title: Taiwan flexes chip diplomacy muscles as it faces pressure to share AI wealth with allies
gist: At SEMICON Taiwan, President Lai Ching-te and Taiwanese chip executives pitched Taiwan as a democratic, reliable AI-chip partner willing to spread manufacturing benefits abroad ('make with Taiwan, not in Taiwan'), while facing US pressure (TSMC's $265 billion Arizona investment, incoming tariffs on non-US-manufacturing chip firms per Commerce Secretary Lutnick, an additional $20 billion in planned Taiwanese US investment) and separate EU courtship via its Chips Act 2.0, all against China's claim that Taiwan is merely a Chinese province.

insights.claim: Taiwan flexed its chip diplomacy at the SEMICON Taiwan trade show, portraying itself as a democratic and reliable supplier for the AI revolution while signaling willingness to share the benefits of its semiconductor prowess with like-minded partners.
insights.speaker: Reuters (via SemiWiki)
insights.so_what: Taiwan explicitly using its chip dominance as a diplomatic bargaining chip signals investors should treat semiconductor policy and foreign-policy alignment as intertwined — geopolitical goodwill toward Taiwan may increasingly track chip-supply-chain concessions.

insights.claim: President Lai Ching-te, unusually speaking at two separate events on the same day at SEMICON Taiwan, said Taiwanese companies were expanding globally to 'let resilience create shared prosperity' and that the island's chip strength was based on democracy and rule of law.
insights.speaker: Lai Ching-te (via SemiWiki)
insights.so_what: A head-of-state making two same-day appearances at a trade show signals unusually high political priority placed on chip diplomacy, useful as a barometer of how central semiconductor leverage has become to Taiwan's foreign policy.

insights.claim: Diplomatically isolated Taiwan has long sought to leverage its tech prowess to garner international support, something Beijing routinely seeks to block, saying the island is merely one of its provinces.
insights.speaker: Reuters (via SemiWiki)
insights.so_what: This frames Taiwan's 'silicon shield' strategy explicitly as a counter to Chinese diplomatic isolation efforts, a persistent geopolitical dynamic relevant to any China-Taiwan tension scenario analysis for semiconductor supply-chain risk.

themes.theme: US pressure and the Arizona/tariff dynamic

insights.claim: Taiwan faces pressure from the United States, its most important international backer and arms supplier, to shift more chip manufacturing there; TSMC is investing $265 billion in factories in the state of Arizona.
insights.speaker: Reuters (via SemiWiki)
insights.so_what: The $265 billion Arizona figure is a concrete, trackable commitment size for assessing how much of TSMC's leading-edge capacity is migrating onshore to the US versus remaining in Taiwan — a key variable for US chip supply-chain resilience and for Taiwan concentration risk.

insights.claim: Economy Minister Kung Ming-hsin, opening the US pavilion at SEMICON, said Taiwanese companies were planning an additional $20 billion of investment in the United States.
insights.speaker: Kung Ming-hsin (via SemiWiki)
insights.so_what: An incremental $20 billion pledge on top of TSMC's existing $265 billion Arizona buildout signals broader Taiwanese industry (beyond TSMC alone) is following the same US-investment trend, worth monitoring for which companies specifically commit.

insights.claim: Taiwan struck a deal with Washington earlier this year to increase US investment in exchange for reduced export tariffs, but uncertainty remains; US Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick told CNBC that semiconductor tariffs were coming for companies that do not make chips in the US, while Bill Frauenhofer, the Commerce Department official overseeing the Taiwan tariff agreement, struck an upbeat tone during SEMICON, calling the partnership "phenomenal."
insights.speaker: Reuters (via SemiWiki)
insights.so_what: The explicit threat of tariffs on chipmakers not manufacturing in the US is a direct policy lever that will keep pushing TSMC, MediaTek, and other Taiwanese firms toward further US capacity commitments — a live regulatory catalyst for near-term capex announcements.
insights.quote: The phenomenal partnership between Taiwan and the U.S. was working. And we really, both of us, have vested interests in terms of making this successful.

insights.claim: Young Liu, chairman of Foxconn — Nvidia's largest AI server maker — said companies now had to 'think about how to make with Taiwan, not in Taiwan; make with Taiwan in the country where the market is,' a view echoed by Tien Wu, chief operating officer of ASE, who called it politically the right thing and said the industry has no choice but to do it.
insights.speaker: Young Liu (via SemiWiki)
insights.so_what: Explicit agreement from both Foxconn's chairman and ASE's COO on 'make with Taiwan' signals this is becoming an industry-wide consensus strategy (not just a TSMC-specific move), implying broader distributed manufacturing investment across Taiwan's whole supply chain, not only leading-edge fabs.
insights.quote: We all have to think about how to make with Taiwan, not in Taiwan; make with Taiwan in the country where the market is

insights.claim: The EU is also seeking greater investment from Taiwanese companies; the bloc sent European Commission official Kilian Gross to SEMICON to pitch the EU's Chips Act 2.0 to Taiwanese officials and companies.
insights.speaker: Reuters (via SemiWiki)
insights.so_what: A dedicated EU pitch for Taiwanese investment via Chips Act 2.0 indicates Europe is competing directly with the US for Taiwanese fab/packaging investment, a third region investors should track alongside US and Japan expansion commitments.

insights.claim: Taiwan has sought closer cooperation with the EU not only because both have strongly backed Ukraine in the war with Russia, but also because both face trade and diplomatic disputes with China; Deputy Foreign Minister Francois Wu told the opening of the French pavilion that Taiwan and France share the values of democracy, freedom and a commitment to a rules-based international order.
insights.speaker: Francois Wu (via SemiWiki)
insights.so_what: Taiwan explicitly linking chip diplomacy to shared Ukraine-war positioning and anti-China friction with the EU shows semiconductor investment negotiations are being bundled with broader geopolitical alignment, relevant for forecasting how EU-Taiwan trade ties evolve alongside Russia/China tensions.
insights.quote: We use technology to connect with the world, not to control it
insights.locator: "EU WANTS INVESTMENT TOO" section, closing quote
